screens.title: Optimizing Python Code
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson we'll focus on the optimizations that matter most: choosing better algorithms and the right data structures. After you profile and find a bottleneck, the most impactful improvements usually come from changing the algorithmic approach or the container types your code uses. For example, replacing repeated linear searches over a list with membership tests on a set often reduces an O(N) cost to an average O(1) cost, which can transform nested operations from slow and quadratic to efficient and linear. We'll also cover memory-aware techniques such as generator expressions and micro-optimizations inside loops like pulling attribute lookups into local variables. Each technique preserves correctness while reducing runtime or memory use. You will see concrete, runnable code examples that compare list membership vs set membership, list comprehensions vs generator expressions, and an efficient word-counter implementation using a generator and collections. Counter. By the end, you'll have a practical checklist for prioritizing optimizations: profile first, reduce algorithmic complexity second, pick the right data structure third, and only then apply micro-optimizations. Consider: if your code doubles in input size, which part will grow fastest — and can you change the algorithm or structure to stop that growth?

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will apply algorithmic complexity analysis to spot inefficient code, select data structures like sets and dictionaries to cut runtime cost of frequent operations, optimize loops and conditionals to reduce per-iteration overhead, and use generator expressions to conserve memory for large streams of data. Each objective maps to practical tasks: analyze the Big O of a routine, replace O(N) membership checks across loops with O(1) lookups, refactor loop bodies to avoid repeated attribute or function lookups, and refactor list-heavy pipelines into generator-based processing when you only need incremental results. These are not theoretical exercises: when input sizes grow, these choices determine whether your program finishes in seconds or never finishes. We'll show concrete examples and a hands-on word counter activity where you implement both an inefficient and an efficient version, then compare results. Keep in mind a common misconception: micro-optimizations are tempting but do not replace selecting the right algorithm or container. Always profile before optimizing so you target the real bottleneck. This objective set is designed to help you prioritize changes that preserve correctness while delivering meaningful speed and memory improvements.

screens.title: Algorithmic Complexity (Big O Notation)
screens.narratorSegment: Big O notation describes how the runtime or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size grows. It isolates the dominant term and ignores constant factors so you can compare growth rates: for example, O(N) grows linearly with input size N, O(N log N) grows faster but far slower than O(N^2), and O(1) indicates constant time independent of N. This matters because when N is large, algorithms with higher-order complexity quickly become impractical. A common concrete example is nested loops over the same collection. Two nested loops that each iterate N times lead to O(N^2) behavior — doubling N quadruples the work. Contrast that with a single loop using a hash-based container for membership checks, which keeps work near O(N). A frequent misconception is to focus only on micro-optimizations such as caching small calculations or using faster built-in functions; these help but cannot make an O(N^2) method perform like an O(N log N) solution. When you profile and identify a hotspot, first ask what the asymptotic complexity is and whether you can choose an algorithm with lower growth. That decision yields orders-of-magnitude improvement as input sizes grow. What part of your code will grow fastest as data increases?

keyIdea.text: Asymptotic complexity predicts scaling behavior — lower-order growth dominates runtime for large inputs.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Algorithmic Complexity
Definition and intuition
Big O captures how cost grows as input scales; focus on dominant terms, not constants.
O(1) — Constant time
Example: dictionary lookup on average.
O(N) — Linear time
Example: scanning a list for membership.
O(N^2) — Quadratic time
Example: nested loops over the same collection.
Key takeaway
When input size increases, asymptotic terms dominate. Replacing algorithms to reduce order yields the largest wins.
Concrete example
Nested membership checks using a list vs a set.
# Inefficient: nested list membership leads to O(M*N)
for item in items_to_check:
  if item in master_list:
    pass

# Efficient approach: convert once to a set, membership checks are O(1) on average
master_set = set(master_list)
for item in items_to_check:
  if item in master_set:
    pass
Misconception: converting to a set inside the loop fixes nothing. Create the set once outside to pay the O(N) cost once, not repeatedly.

screens.title: Membership Tests: list vs set
screens.narratorSegment: Membership testing is a small-looking operation that often drives large costs when used repeatedly. In Python, checking an item in a list requires scanning elements until a match is found or the list ends, which is O(N) in the worst case. In contrast, sets and dictionaries use a hash-table implementation, making membership checks average O(1). That difference transforms the total cost of repeated membership checks. For example, if you check M items against a master collection of size N inside a loop, doing a list membership inside the loop yields O(M*N) work. But if you convert the master collection to a set once outside the loop, you pay O(N) to build the set plus O(M) for checks, giving O(N + M) overall. An important practical detail: converting a large collection to a set has its own cost, so profile whether repeated membership checks justify that one-time conversion. Avoid converting the collection inside the loop — a common mistake that undoes the benefit. Think about the ratio of M to N and frequency of checks when making the choice. Membership Tests: list vs set means prefer set or dict for frequent membership checks; build the hash-based container once outside repeated checks.. In practical terms, compare performance and complexity for frequent membership checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Membership Tests
List membership (O(N))
Linear scan: cost grows with collection size.
# Example worst case check
large_list = list(range(1_000_000))
start = time.time()
(1_000_000 - 1) in large_list
end = time.time()
print(end - start)
Use lists for ordered collections, small sizes, or cases where membership checks are rare.
Set membership (avg O(1))
Hash table lookup gives constant average time.
large_set = set(range(1_000_000))
start = time.time()
(1_000_000 - 1) in large_set
end = time.time()
print(end - start)
Build the set once outside loops. When membership tests are the hotspot, switching to a set is typically the highest payoff change.
Common mistake
Converting to a list inside a loop or recreating a set each iteration loses the asymptotic advantage.
Pro tip
If building the set is expensive and queries are few, measure first; a set is worth it when queries are numerous or repeated.
Key Takeaway

Switching to hash-based containers reduces repeated membership cost dramatically when checks are frequent.

screens.title: Avoid building lists for large streams
screens.narratorSegment: List comprehensions are concise and often faster for creating an entire list, but they materialize the whole sequence in memory. For large values of N, that memory allocation can be huge and may raise out-of-memory errors. Generator expressions are a lazy alternative: they produce one item at a time and never hold the entire sequence. The practical trade-off is that a generator cannot be indexed or reused unless you convert it, and some built-in functions will evaluate it eagerly. Use a generator when you only need to iterate or stream results, such as computing an aggregate or feeding a pipeline. A concrete example from the chapter compares creating ten million doubled numbers with a list comprehension and a generator expression while reporting sizes via the getsizeof function. The list occupies megabytes, whereas the generator object remains small because it only stores the iteration state. A common misunderstanding is thinking generators are always slower; they can be faster overall because they avoid allocation and garbage collection. Choose generators for memory-bound workloads and list comprehensions for when you need random access or multiple passes.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › List vs Generator
List comprehension example
Creates the full list in memory.
N = 10_000_000
list_comp = [i * 2 for i in range(N)]
print(sys.getsizeof(list_comp) / (1024*1024), 'MB')
del list_comp
Use when you need random access or multiple passes over the data and memory is adequate.
Generator expression example
Creates an iterator that yields values on demand without holding them all.
gen_exp = (i * 2 for i in range(N))
print(sys.getsizeof(gen_exp) / (1024*1024), 'MB')
# To consume: sum(gen_exp) or iterate in a loop
Analogy: a conveyor belt producing items one by one instead of stacking them in a bin.
When to use generator
Streaming large files, piping to aggregators, or memory-limited environments.
Misconception
Thinking generators are always slower; they often reduce overall time by avoiding heavy allocations.
Key Takeaway

Use list comprehensions for small-to-moderate sequences and generators for very large streams you process once.

screens.title: Optimizing Loop Bodies
screens.narratorSegment: Loop performance often improves dramatically by reducing the work done on each iteration. A simple pattern is to hoist invariant computations — move any calculation, attribute lookup, or object creation that does not depend on the loop variable out of the loop. For example, repeatedly accessing self. multiplier inside a tight loop triggers attribute lookup cost every iteration. Assigning that attribute to a local variable once before the loop and using the local name avoids repeated lookups. Another common example is avoiding repeated function calls that return the same value; call the function once and reuse the result when appropriate. Always confirm that moving code outside the loop preserves correctness; if the value can change inside the loop, hoisting would be wrong. A misconception is expecting huge gains from hoisting in all cases; the benefit matters most in tight loops with many iterations. Profiling before and after a change shows whether the micro-optimization is beneficial. This pattern reduces per-iteration overhead and compounds when iterations are numerous, producing meaningful speedups without changing algorithmic complexity. Optimizing Loop Bodies means move work that doesn't depend on the loop variable out of the loop to reduce per-iteration cost.. In practical terms, hoist invariants and reduce expensive operations per iteration. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Optimizing Loop Bodies
Example: attribute lookup hoist
Reduce repeated attribute access inside tight loops.
class MyProcessor:
    def __init__(self, multiplier):
        self.multiplier = multiplier

    def process_items_bad(self, items):
        results = []
        for item in items:
            results.append(item * self.multiplier)  # attribute lookup each iteration
        return results

    def process_items_good(self, items):
        results = []
        local_multiplier = self.multiplier  # hoisted once
        for item in items:
            results.append(item * local_multiplier)
        return results
This micro-optimization is most valuable in tight loops with many iterations. Always validate with a profiler to confirm real impact.
Supporting tips
  • Cache expensive lookups or function results when they are invariant.
  • Avoid allocating objects inside loops when a reusable object suffices.
  • Prefer local variables over repeated global or attribute access.
Key Takeaway

Small per-iteration savings multiply across many iterations; hoist invariants and cache results when safe.

screens.title: Common Mistakes and Misconceptions
screens.narratorSegment: A frequent mistake is optimizing without profiling. Developers often change code based on intuition and may improve a non-critical part while leaving the real hotspot untouched. Profiling pinpoints where your program spends time and gives confidence your changes matter. Another common error is changing data structures without updating code semantics. For example, switching from list to set removes order and duplicates; if your algorithm relies on order or repeated elements, correctness breaks. Also avoid converting containers inside loops — doing so negates the asymptotic advantage. When making optimizations, add tests that capture current behavior and edge cases before you refactor. That way you can verify correctness after the change. Premature micro-optimizations that trade clarity for negligible speed can hurt maintainability. Finally, be mindful of memory vs speed trade-offs: sometimes you trade a bit more memory to avoid expensive recomputation, and sometimes you accept slower occasional recompute to save memory. The choice should be guided by profiling and the operational constraints of your environment. Common Mistakes and Misconceptions means profile to find bottlenecks, add tests to keep behavior stable, and avoid premature micro-optimizations that reduce clarity.. In practical terms, premature optimization and incorrect refactors. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Common Mistakes
Mistakes to avoid
Target real problems and preserve correctness.
Optimizing without profiling
You may waste effort on non-critical code. Use a profiler to measure hotspots before changing code.
Changing structure without tests
Refactor only after adding tests to lock in expected behavior so you can safely verify the optimization.
Converting inside loops
Creating new containers per iteration negates any asymptotic advantage; build once outside instead.
Ignoring semantic changes
Switching to a set removes order and duplicates. Ensure the algorithm remains correct after changing structures.
Key Takeaway

Measure first, test during, and validate after. Prefer algorithmic change over micro-tweaks when possible.

screens.title: Optimize a Word Counter — Inefficient Version
screens.narratorSegment: The starter word counter accumulates all words into a single list, then counts them with a manual dictionary and finally sorts to find the top ten. This approach uses a lot of memory because it stores every token extracted from the file. It also repeats work: building and extending lists per line rather than streaming words into a counting structure. The sorting step also sorts all unique words to find the top ten, which is unnecessarily expensive when you only need the most common items. The key lessons are: don't create large intermediate structures when you can stream, use specialized data structures implemented in C when possible, and avoid sorting the entire dataset when more efficient APIs exist. The starter code is helpful to illustrate the failure modes: high memory use, repeated allocations, and extra computational steps that add up with large inputs. We'll refactor this flow into a generator-driven, Counter-based implementation that streams words and uses a built-in most_common function to return the top ten efficiently. Optimize a Word Counter — Inefficient Version means accumulating all words in memory and manually counting then sorting is wasteful for large files; streaming and counter are better.. In practical terms, understand why the starter approach is slow and memory-heavy. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 12 › Chapter 12.3 › Inefficient Word Counter
Starter code pattern
Accumulating all words then counting and sorting.
def count_words_inefficient(filepath):
    all_words = []
    with open(filepath, 'r') as f:
        for line in f:
            words_in_line = re.findall(r'\b\w+\b', line.lower())
            all_words.extend(words_in_line)

    word_counts = {}
    for word in all_words:
        word_counts[word] = word_counts.get(word, 0) + 1

    sorted_counts = sorted(word_counts.items(), key=lambda item: item[1], reverse=True)
    return sorted_counts[:10]
Problem
Creates large intermediate list and manually counts then sorts everything.
Impact
High memory usage and unnecessary work for huge files.
What to do
Stream words and use collections.Counter.most_common to avoid full sorts and reduce memory.

Generator + Counter
Stream words and let Counter handle counting efficiently.
def count_words_efficient(filepath):
    def word_generator(path):
        with open(path, 'r') as f:
            for line in f:
                yield from (word for word in re.findall(r'\b\w+\b', line.lower()))

    word_counts = Counter(word_generator(filepath))
    return word_counts.most_common(10)
Why it works
Generator avoids storing all tokens; Counter is optimized in C for counting.
Verification

Key Takeaway

screens.title: Memory vs Time Trade-offs
screens.narratorSegment: Optimizations often involve trade-offs between time and memory. Building an index or additional cache can speed repeated operations at the cost of extra memory. For example, converting a list to a set consumes additional memory for the hash table but reduces membership test time from O(N) to average O(1). Conversely, avoiding a persistent cache and recomputing values can save memory but cost C P U time. The right balance depends on workload and environment: memory-constrained systems favor streaming and generators, while latency-sensitive services may prefer precomputed caches. A concrete way to make the decision is to measure both memory usage and runtime before and after a change. Use sys. getsizeof for rough object size, but remember it does not account for referenced objects; combine measurements with realistic profiling under production-like loads. A common misconception is assuming more memory always means faster code; sometimes memory allocations and GC pressure add overhead, so measure end-to-end. Reflect on operational constraints and pick the pattern that gives acceptable performance while staying within memory limits. screens.title: Preserving Correctness While Optimizing
screens.narratorSegment: Safety is critical during optimization: faster code must remain correct. Create regression tests that capture expected outputs and edge cases before changing implementation. For the word-counter example, a unit test that verifies the top ten words for a small sample file gives confidence the new generator-based implementation matches the old result. When switching data structures, check behavioral differences such as ordering or duplicate handling. If you change a list to a set, tests should verify that order was not relied upon or update expectations accordingly. After refactoring, run the test suite and add performance measurements to ensure the optimization yields the intended benefit. If performance regresses on some platforms, keep the previous implementation behind a feature flag or provide a fallback. A common misconception is to trust manual inspection; automated tests remove doubt and allow continuous improvement. Ultimately, optimization should be iterative: profile, test, refactor, measure, and repeat until the performance and correctness goals are met. screens.title: Key Concepts — Part 1
screens.narratorSegment: Keep these core ideas in mind when optimizing Python code. First, algorithmic complexity is the primary lever: prefer algorithms with lower asymptotic growth to gain the largest improvements. Second, sets and dictionaries provide average constant-time membership checks due to their hash-table nature, making them the right choice when membership tests are frequent. Third, list comprehensions allocate full lists and can use significant memory for large inputs, whereas generator expressions yield items lazily and keep memory usage low. These concepts guide everyday decisions: pick the right data structure, choose lazy evaluation when streaming, and reduce asymptotic costs before applying micro-optimizations. A quick mental checklist — profile first, then algorithm/data-structure change, then micro-optimizations — helps you focus effort where it pays off. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson we'll focus on the optimizations that matter most: choosing better algorithms and the right data structures. After you profile and find a bottleneck, the most impactful improvements usually come from changing the algorithmic approach or the container types your code uses. For example, replacing repeated linear searches over a list with membership tests on a set often reduces an O(N) cost to an average O(1) cost, which can transform nested operations from slow and quadratic to efficient and linear. We'll also cover memory-aware techniques such as generator expressions and micro-optimizations inside loops like pulling attribute lookups into local variables. Each technique preserves correctness while reducing runtime or memory use. You will see concrete, runnable code examples that compare list membership vs set membership, list comprehensions vs generator expressions, and an efficient word-counter implementation using a generator and collections. Counter. By the end, you'll have a practical checklist for prioritizing optimizations: profile first, reduce algorithmic complexity second, pick the right data structure third, and only then apply micro-optimizations. Consider: if your code doubles in input size, which part will grow fastest — and can you change the algorithm or structure to stop that growth?

By the end of this chapter you will apply algorithmic complexity analysis to spot inefficient code, select data structures like sets and dictionaries to cut runtime cost of frequent operations, optimize loops and conditionals to reduce per-iteration overhead, and use generator expressions to conserve memory for large streams of data. Each objective maps to practical tasks: analyze the Big O of a routine, replace O(N) membership checks across loops with O(1) lookups, refactor loop bodies to avoid repeated attribute or function lookups, and refactor list-heavy pipelines into generator-based processing when you only need incremental results. These are not theoretical exercises: when input sizes grow, these choices determine whether your program finishes in seconds or never finishes. We'll show concrete examples and a hands-on word counter activity where you implement both an inefficient and an efficient version, then compare results. Keep in mind a common misconception: micro-optimizations are tempting but do not replace selecting the right algorithm or container. Always profile before optimizing so you target the real bottleneck. This objective set is designed to help you prioritize changes that preserve correctness while delivering meaningful speed and memory improvements.

These practical objectives translate to small code changes you can apply immediately. You'll practice converting repeated list-based membership tests into set-backed checks and measuring the change. You'll implement a memory-conscious pipeline using generator expressions and collections. Counter to compute word frequencies without keeping all words in memory. You'll refactor loops to move invariant computations outside the iteration and measure the difference. Finally, you'll learn to validate that optimizations preserve behavior by adding tests and comparing outputs before and after refactoring. A common pitfall is changing implementation without regression tests and introducing subtle bugs; we'll show the safe pattern: profile, write a test to capture current behavior, refactor, then re-run tests and compare performance results. These hands-on skills ensure optimizations are both effective and safe in production code. As you practice, focus on changes that reduce asymptotic cost first, then fine-tune micro costs if necessary.

Big O notation describes how the runtime or memory of an algorithm grows as the input size grows. It isolates the dominant term and ignores constant factors so you can compare growth rates: for example, O(N) grows linearly with input size N, O(N log N) grows faster but far slower than O(N^2), and O(1) indicates constant time independent of N. This matters because when N is large, algorithms with higher-order complexity quickly become impractical. A common concrete example is nested loops over the same collection. Two nested loops that each iterate N times lead to O(N^2) behavior — doubling N quadruples the work. Contrast that with a single loop using a hash-based container for membership checks, which keeps work near O(N). A frequent misconception is to focus only on micro-optimizations such as caching small calculations or using faster built-in functions; these help but cannot make an O(N^2) method perform like an O(N log N) solution. When you profile and identify a hotspot, first ask what the asymptotic complexity is and whether you can choose an algorithm with lower growth. That decision yields orders-of-magnitude improvement as input sizes grow. What part of your code will grow fastest as data increases?

Membership testing is a small-looking operation that often drives large costs when used repeatedly. In Python, checking an item in a list requires scanning elements until a match is found or the list ends, which is O(N) in the worst case. In contrast, sets and dictionaries use a hash-table implementation, making membership checks average O(1). That difference transforms the total cost of repeated membership checks. For example, if you check M items against a master collection of size N inside a loop, doing a list membership inside the loop yields O(M*N) work. But if you convert the master collection to a set once outside the loop, you pay O(N) to build the set plus O(M) for checks, giving O(N + M) overall. An important practical detail: converting a large collection to a set has its own cost, so profile whether repeated membership checks justify that one-time conversion. Avoid converting the collection inside the loop — a common mistake that undoes the benefit. Think about the ratio of M to N and frequency of checks when making the choice. Membership Tests: list vs set means prefer set or dict for frequent membership checks; build the hash-based container once outside repeated checks.. In practical terms, compare performance and complexity for frequent membership checks. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

List comprehensions are concise and often faster for creating an entire list, but they materialize the whole sequence in memory. For large values of N, that memory allocation can be huge and may raise out-of-memory errors. Generator expressions are a lazy alternative: they produce one item at a time and never hold the entire sequence. The practical trade-off is that a generator cannot be indexed or reused unless you convert it, and some built-in functions will evaluate it eagerly. Use a generator when you only need to iterate or stream results, such as computing an aggregate or feeding a pipeline. A concrete example from the chapter compares creating ten million doubled numbers with a list comprehension and a generator expression while reporting sizes via the getsizeof function. The list occupies megabytes, whereas the generator object remains small because it only stores the iteration state. A common misunderstanding is thinking generators are always slower; they can be faster overall because they avoid allocation and garbage collection. Choose generators for memory-bound workloads and list comprehensions for when you need random access or multiple passes.

Loop performance often improves dramatically by reducing the work done on each iteration. A simple pattern is to hoist invariant computations — move any calculation, attribute lookup, or object creation that does not depend on the loop variable out of the loop. For example, repeatedly accessing self. multiplier inside a tight loop triggers attribute lookup cost every iteration. Assigning that attribute to a local variable once before the loop and using the local name avoids repeated lookups. Another common example is avoiding repeated function calls that return the same value; call the function once and reuse the result when appropriate. Always confirm that moving code outside the loop preserves correctness; if the value can change inside the loop, hoisting would be wrong. A misconception is expecting huge gains from hoisting in all cases; the benefit matters most in tight loops with many iterations. Profiling before and after a change shows whether the micro-optimization is beneficial. This pattern reduces per-iteration overhead and compounds when iterations are numerous, producing meaningful speedups without changing algorithmic complexity. Profiling pinpoints where your program spends time and gives confidence your changes matter. Another common error is changing data structures without updating code semantics. Keep these core ideas in mind when optimizing Python code. First, algorithmic complexity is the primary lever: prefer algorithms with lower asymptotic growth to gain the largest improvements. Second, sets and dictionaries provide average constant-time membership checks due to their hash-table nature, making them the right choice when membership tests are frequent. Third, list comprehensions allocate full lists and can use significant memory for large inputs, whereas generator expressions yield items lazily and keep memory usage low. These concepts guide everyday decisions: pick the right data structure, choose lazy evaluation when streaming, and reduce asymptotic costs before applying micro-optimizations.
